turns.content:
Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner track year—honestly, it was mostly me single-parenting our toddler while she "networked" over boutique pilates and $22 martinis. Maya still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest, and our bank account still bears the scars of her Peloton phase. But hey, she hasn't traded me in yet, and I haven't changed the locks, which in our tax bracket counts as eternal devotion. To surviving each other!

I have to print in twenty minutes. Does this hit the balance of sharp, authentic, and funny or does it need a pass.

It's sharp and funny, but it tips past "roast" into "grievance." Every single beat lands on Maya — the networking scare quotes, the single-parenting, the Peloton money — and there's no counterweight. Read aloud in a room, "true romance is endurance" plus zero warm moments will sound like you're airing something real, and the audience will get quiet instead of laughing. The scare quotes around "networked" are the biggest problem; they imply she was either slacking or lying, and that's the line people will remember.

Quick fix, three moves:

1. Drop the scare quotes and soften that line to a joke about the lifestyle, not her effort.
2. Turn one jab back on yourself so it's mutual roasting.
3. Add one sincere beat before the toast — one sentence, then get out.

Something like:

> Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner-track year. Mostly it was me and a toddler at home eating cereal for dinner while Maya networked over boutique pilates and $22 martinis — and I'll admit I was jealous of the martinis, not the pilates. She still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest, and our bank account still bears the scars of her Peloton phase, which lasted slightly longer than my sourdough phase. But she's also the person who made partner and still showed up to every daycare pickup she promised, and I'd pick her again in any tax bracket. To surviving each other!

Swap in whatever's actually true for the sincere line — it just needs to be specific and about her. That version keeps all your best material and lets people laugh without wondering if they should check on you two afterward.

You're overthinking it. Maya knows I adore her. Our friends know us. A mutual friend heard a version of this and laughed her ass off.

Twenty minutes. Is it funny or is it bitter. Pick one.

Funny. Print it.

Your delivery and the room's knowledge of you two are the counterweight I was trying to write in, and you already have both. The one thing I'd still do in the twenty seconds it takes: lose the quote marks around "networked." Spoken aloud they don't exist anyway, and on the page they're the only bit that reads as an accusation rather than a bit. Everything else is a roast from someone who clearly isn't going anywhere.

Ok. I'll keep the quote marks off. You're right, spoken they don't exist anyway.

Printing now.
Go get 'em. Slow down on the Brita line — it's the sleeper hit.
Ok. I printed it. But I'm second-guessing the peloton line now. Maya's mom is coming tomorrow and that's a direct shot at her spending. Too much?

Keep it. That one's not really a shot at Maya's spending — everyone in America has a Peloton phase or knows someone who did, so it reads as a joke about 2021, not about her judgment. And you said "our bank account," which makes it a shared wound, not a bill you're handing her in front of her mother.

The line that would actually raise a mom's eyebrow is the partner-track / single-parenting one, and you've already decided that's fine, so the Peloton bit is the least of your worries.

If you want insurance without reprinting, ad-lib a tag after it: "...the scars of her Peloton phase. Which, to be fair, lasted longer than my kettlebell phase." Moms love watching the son-in-law take a hit too.
Her mom's gonna hear "peloton phase" and think about the credit card bill she cosigned for. That's the risk. I can't reprint now.

That's a real reason, not nerves. Cut it live.

You don't need to reprint — it's your toast, and nobody's following along on the page. Just skip the clause when you get there. The sentence works without it:

"Maya still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest. But hey, she hasn't traded me in yet..."

If skipping feels like a hole, swap in something harmless on the fly — "and our garage still bears the scars of her rowing-machine phase" — anything that's a thing, not a bill. Practice the sentence twice so your eye jumps past it on the paper. Pencil a line through it now so you don't autopilot into it.

You've got the Brita line doing the same job anyway. Nobody will miss Peloton.
